title: DHM Supplement: What It Is, Benefits & Dosage Guide
excerpt: How much DHM to take, when, and which product gives you that dose, based on what the research actually used.
metaDescription: How much DHM to take: there is no official dose. Products give 300 mg or 1,000 mg, and the human capsule trial used 600 mg a day. Timing, safety and what to buy.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
There is no established human dose of DHM (dihydromyricetin). Most products put either 300 mg or 1,000 mg in a serving, and the one controlled human trial of DHM capsules we have found used 600 mg a day, taken as two doses, for three months. A sensible plan is to start with 300 mg, go up to 600 mg if you want more, and stay within the label. Nobody has tested in people whether it works better before, during or after drinking.

If you already know how much you want, here is the cheapest way we know to get each amount:

| Amount | What to buy | Per night |
|---|---|---|
| 300 mg, to start | [DHM Depot](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0767N448Q?tag=dhmguide-20), 1 serving | $0.40 |
| 600 mg | [DHM Depot](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0767N448Q?tag=dhmguide-20), 2 servings | $0.80 |
| 1,000 mg | [NusaPure](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08B32XBRB?tag=dhmguide-20), 1 serving | $0.48 |
| 1,000 mg plus L-cysteine | [No Days Wasted](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), 1 serving | $1.93 |

Costs are the list price divided by the servings in the bottle, using the prices we last recorded. Amazon prices move, so check the listing. Our [DHM supplement reviews](/reviews) rank every brand we track by dose and price per serving, and the [comparison tool](/compare) puts any two side by side.

> **This is not medical advice.** DHM is a dietary supplement, and the FDA does not check supplements for safety or effectiveness before they go on sale. Ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicine (especially sedatives, sleep aids, diabetes medicine or blood thinners), are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, or are under 21.

## What DHM is

DHM is a flavonoid, a type of plant compound. Most of the DHM sold in capsules is extracted from vine tea (*Ampelopsis grossedentata*), a plant used in Chinese herbal tea that contains a lot of it. It is also found in the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), which is where the compound's reputation as a drinking remedy comes from. Our page on the [Japanese raisin tree and DHM](/never-hungover/dhm-japanese-raisin-tree-complete-guide) covers that history.

The interest in DHM as a hangover supplement traces back to one 2012 study in rats, covered below. Since then it has been sold in two forms: plain DHM capsules or tablets, and "hangover formulas" that add other ingredients such as L-cysteine, milk thistle and B vitamins.

## Where the dose numbers come from

When you see a confident number for how much DHM to take, it almost always traces back to a manufacturer's label, not a study. Here is what the published research actually used.

The one controlled human trial of DHM capsules we have found was run at the Third Military Medical University in Chongqing, China, and published in *Pharmacological Research* in 2015 ([Chen et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26032587/)). Sixty adults with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease took either two 150 mg capsules of DHM twice a day (600 mg a day in total) or a placebo for three months. The DHM group ended with lower liver enzymes, blood glucose and LDL cholesterol than the placebo group. That is a real result, but it was about fatty liver, the participants were not drinking for the study, and nobody measured hangovers.

A second trial from the same city gave 80 adults with type 2 diabetes vine tea containing about 970 mg of DHM a day for a month, against a placebo tea with the DHM removed ([Ran et al., 2019, *European Journal of Clinical Nutrition*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30089792/)). Fasting blood glucose fell in the DHM group. Again, there was no alcohol involved and no hangover measures.

The study that made DHM famous was done in rats at UCLA ([Shen et al., 2012, *Journal of Neuroscience*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22219299/)). The rats got 1 mg of DHM per kilogram of body weight as an injection into the abdomen, and it reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal. An injection skips the gut, and rat doses do not convert neatly into human capsules, so this study tells you DHM is worth researching. It does not tell you how much to swallow.

A later study from the same group, by then at the University of Southern California, gave mice 5 mg/kg of DHM by injection every day for eight weeks of heavy alcohol feeding and found that the livers of DHM-treated mice kept more of their normal energy production ([Silva et al., 2021, *Alcohol*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7902334/)). Again, mice and injections.

The human hangover trials you may see cited are about a different product. A 2024 crossover trial in *Foods* gave 25 adults drinks made with Japanese raisin tree fruit extract, mixed with either kudzu (*Pueraria*) or glutathione yeast ([Lee et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11675335/)). The drinks reduced stomach and gut symptoms compared with placebo. They were drinks, not DHM capsules, they mixed the raisin tree extract with other ingredients, and several of the authors work for the drink's maker, Kwangdong Pharmaceutical.

So the 300 mg and 1,000 mg servings on the shelf are choices made by manufacturers. We have not found a study showing either amount works better than the other for hangovers. You will see dosing charts by body weight on many sites, including an earlier version of this page. No human study has tested DHM by body weight, and we have removed that chart.

## How much DHM to take: a practical plan

Given that evidence, this is how we would approach it.

Start with 300 mg the first time. A low first dose tells you whether DHM upsets your stomach or makes you drowsy alongside alcohol, without committing to a large amount. DHM Depot and Toniiq Ease both come in 300 mg servings.

If you want more, 600 mg is the most defensible next step, because it is the daily total used in that capsule trial. Two servings of a 300 mg product gets you there.

A 1,000 mg serving, which is what NusaPure, Double Wood, No Days Wasted and Cheers all list, is not known to be better or worse than 600 mg. It is simply the most common size on Amazon. If you already own a 1,000 mg product, there is no reason to throw it out.

Two things to avoid. Don't add DHM from two products on the same night, for example a capsule plus a DHM drink, because the amounts add up and you lose track of what you took. And don't go above what the label says. There is no established upper limit in people, which is a reason for caution, not a license to experiment.

## When to take DHM

No study in people has compared taking DHM before drinking with taking it during or after. Anyone who tells you that one timing is a certain percentage more effective is quoting a number that nobody measured.

Directions also vary from brand to brand, so read your label. The case for taking it before or while you drink is only reasoning: if DHM affects how the body handles alcohol, it would need to be in your system while the alcohol is. Taking it the next morning, once the alcohol is mostly gone, makes the least sense.

What matters more is picking one routine and sticking to it. If you change the dose, the timing and how much you drink all at once, you will never know whether the DHM did anything. Our [DHM timing guide](/never-hungover/when-to-take-dhm-timing-guide-2025) goes through the common routines in more detail.

## Reading the label: servings, capsules and extracts

The dose on the front of the bottle and the dose you swallow are not always the same thing. Three things to check on the supplement facts panel:

1. How many capsules make one serving. Toniiq Ease, for example, lists 300 mg of DHM in a serving of three capsules. If you take one capsule, you are getting about 100 mg.
2. Whether the number is DHM or a plant extract. Cheers lists about 1,200 mg of vine tea extract at 98% DHM, which works out to roughly 1,176 mg of DHM. That is close enough. A label that lists an extract weight with no DHM percentage tells you nothing about the actual dose.
3. Whether the product says DHM at all. "Hovenia dulcis extract" or "Japanese raisin tree extract" is not the same as dihydromyricetin. A plain plant extract can contain very little of it.

If the label hides DHM inside a "proprietary blend" with one combined weight, you cannot know your dose, and we would pick a different product. Our [price per mg comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-price-per-mg-compared) shows how to work out what each brand actually costs per 100 mg of DHM.

## How often you can take it

We don't know how safe frequent, long-term DHM use is. The longest controlled use in people that we have found is the three-month fatty-liver trial above, at 600 mg a day. Most people who use DHM take it only on nights they drink, which keeps total exposure low.

If you find yourself taking it most days, that says more about the drinking than the supplement, and it is worth talking to a doctor. Our guide on [taking DHM every day](/never-hungover/can-you-take-dhm-every-day-long-term-guide-2025) covers what is and isn't known.

## Side effects and who should skip it

People who use DHM mostly report mild problems: an upset stomach, nausea, or feeling drowsy, which is hard to separate from the alcohol itself. The human trials so far have been small and short, so rare side effects would not have shown up.

Check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking DHM if any of these apply to you:

- You take sedatives, sleep aids or anti-anxiety medicine. In the 2012 rat study, DHM acted at the same site on brain receptors as benzodiazepines such as Valium. Combining it with those drugs and alcohol could add to drowsiness.
- You take diabetes medicine. DHM lowered blood glucose in both the fatty-liver and diabetes trials, so it could add to the effect of glucose-lowering drugs.
- You take blood thinners or other drugs processed by the liver. Interaction data in people is very limited.
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver or kidney disease. There is no safety data for these groups.

DHM is not a treatment for alcohol poisoning or withdrawal. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has a seizure. Shaking, sweating and a racing heart when you stop drinking after several heavy days can be withdrawal, which needs a doctor, not a supplement. Our [DHM safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-safety-complete-guide-2025) and [medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) go into more detail.

If you have decided DHM is reasonable for you, the [reviews page](/reviews) lists each brand's dose, price per serving and ingredients in one table.

## Does DHM work for hangovers?

We have not found a published, placebo-controlled trial of DHM capsules for hangovers in people. The evidence is rat and mouse research, the fatty-liver and diabetes trials, which didn't involve drinking, and the raisin-tree-extract drinks, which reduced gut symptoms but were a different product.

Plenty of people say DHM helps them, and that counts for something. But it is hard to separate from the other things people do on a night they planned for, such as eating first, drinking water and stopping earlier. DHM is also poorly absorbed when swallowed, at least in rats, which is one reason the animal results may not carry over.

Treat it as a reasonable thing to try, not a guarantee. That is also the best argument for buying a cheap, plain product: if it does nothing for you, you have lost less. Our review of [whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) and our summary of the [human DHM trials](/never-hungover/dhm-randomized-controlled-trials) cover the evidence study by study.

## Which product fits your dose

All of these list DHM in milligrams on the label. Prices are the ones we last recorded.

[DHM Depot](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0767N448Q?tag=dhmguide-20) is the easiest way to control your dose: 300 mg per serving, 50 servings for $19.95, which is $0.40 a serving. Two servings for 600 mg cost $0.80 a night. It is made by Double Wood Supplements. Our [DHM Depot review](/never-hungover/dhm-depot-review-2025) has more.

[NusaPure DHM 1,000 mg](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08B32XBRB?tag=dhmguide-20) is the cheapest DHM per milligram we track: 60 servings of 1,000 mg for $28.99, or $0.48 a serving. The catch is that it only comes in 1,000 mg servings. See our [NusaPure review](/never-hungover/nusapure-dhm-review-analysis).

[Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) also lists 1,000 mg per serving, at $23.95 for 30 servings ($0.80 each). It costs more per milligram than NusaPure but has far more reviews behind it. Our [Double Wood review](/never-hungover/double-wood-dhm-review-analysis) covers it.

[No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, B vitamins and electrolytes to 1,000 mg of DHM, at $28.99 for 15 servings ($1.93 each). L-cysteine has one small human trial behind it: 19 men in Finland, where 1,200 mg was linked to less nausea and headache ([Eriksson et al., 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32808029/)). You are paying about four times NusaPure's price per milligram of DHM for the extras. More in our [No Days Wasted review](/never-hungover/no-days-wasted-dhm-review-analysis).

[Toniiq Ease](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07S448GTT?tag=dhmguide-20) pairs 300 mg of DHM with reishi mushroom and milk thistle, $24.97 for 40 servings ($0.62 each). Each serving is three capsules. It suits someone more interested in a general liver formula than in a dose for one night out.

[Cheers Restore](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B079P7FXTW?tag=dhmguide-20) is the best-known brand, with the most reviews, but at $34.99 for 12 servings it costs $2.92 a serving. Read the current label, because the capsules per serving can differ between versions of the product.

To see these with ratings, pros and cons in one place, use our [DHM supplement reviews](/reviews). To compare two directly, use the [comparison tool](/compare).

## Frequently asked questions

### How much DHM should I take?

There is no official dose. Most products give 300 mg or 1,000 mg per serving. The one controlled human trial of DHM capsules we have found used 600 mg a day, split into two doses. Start with 300 mg, go up to 600 mg if you want more, and don't exceed the label.

### Should I take DHM before or after drinking?

No study in people has compared the two. If you take it, taking it before or while you drink makes the most sense, because that is when alcohol is in your system. Taking it the next morning makes the least sense.

### Does DHM dosage depend on body weight?

Not that anyone has shown. No human study has tested DHM doses by body weight, so charts that give one dose for 130 lbs and another for 180 lbs are guesses.

### Can you take DHM every day?

The longest controlled human use we know of is a three-month trial at 600 mg a day in people with fatty liver disease. There is no long-term safety data beyond that. Most people take it only on nights they drink.

### What is the maximum safe dose of DHM?

No upper limit has been established in people. Stay within the dose on the label, and don't combine DHM from two products on the same night.

### Is DHM proven to work for hangovers?

No. The research is mostly in rats and mice. The 2024 human trial people cite tested drinks made with Japanese raisin tree extract, not DHM capsules, and found fewer stomach symptoms. DHM is a reasonable thing to try, not a proven treatment.
